segments.text: The report says successful.
How much code actually ran?
Today we will read unit test results as
evidence, not as a green decoration.
Our original Python 3.10 lab checks
empty suites, skipped bodies, expected
failures, unexpected successes,
subtests, and fixture cleanup.
60 outer harness checks pass because
they verify the exact outcomes of these
small inner examples.
Several inner examples deliberately
fail. We will never count those failures
as passing application tests.
The central question is simple. Which
result field supports the sentence we
want to say?
A zero failure count can coexist with no
tests, skipped work, or an unexpected
success.
Keep the collection, execution, and
reporting layers separate before
deciding whether a result should let
your project continue.
Run an empty test suite through our
runner.
The result reports zero tests run, zero
failures, and zero errors. Its was
successful method returns true.
That is the framework answering its own
success rule. It has not invented a
minimum useful test count for your
project.
A selector typo, an empty custom suite,
or the wrong search path can therefore
produce a reassuring result without
exercising the intended behavior.
Our example deliberately constructs the
empty suite, so its cause is known.
In a real project, inspect collection
and command context before blaming the
framework.
A minimum count can catch this
particular emptiness, but a nonzero
count still cannot prove that you
selected the correct tests or checked
the important assertions.
Our next case checks that 2 + 3 = 5. It
runs once and succeeds with no failure
or error.
Unlike the suite, this result includes
an executed test body and a concrete
assertion, but that difference does not
authorize a larger claim. The test has
not exercised every arithmetic input,
your service, or all code paths in the
repository.
Test count is not assertion count
either. One method can contain several
assertions, a loop, or no useful
assertion at all.
Our tiny example names its purpose, so
the report is easy to interpret.
When reviewing a green suite, ask what
input reached which behavior and which
observation would have failed if that
behavior were wrong.
A report summarizes results. It cannot
supply missing test intent.
Decorate our test with skip and a clear
syntactic reason. Its body would raise
an error if executed, but that body's
never run.
The report still has tests run equal to
one, skipped equal to one, and
successful equal to true.
Here, tests run is a framework result
counter, not a promise that every
counted body completed.
This is why merely requiring a non-zero
test count does not solve the skipped
work problem.
Skipping can be legitimate for an
unavailable environment, but it should
remain visible as missing execution.
Do not remove a justified skip just to
make a dashboard look stronger. Decide
what your project permits, preserve the
reason, and distinguish accepted absence
from a successful behavior check.
Mark a test as expected failure, then
deliberately assert that 2 + 3 = 6.
The test method runs and its assertion
fails, but the result records one
expected failure rather than one
ordinary failure.
The overall result is successful under
unit tests rule.
That does not mean the arithmetic claim
became correct.
The decorator tells the runner how to
classify a known failure.
Treat this marker as a visible
maintained exception, not as a way to
turn an inconvenient broken test into
proof.
If your workflow allows expected
failures, identify the known issue and
the reason.
In this teaching fixture, the expected
failure is the lesson itself.
Our outer harness passes only because it
observes that precise classification.
Keep the expected failure decorator, but
repair the assertion to expect five.
Now the method succeeds, yet the report
records an unexpected success, and the
overall result is unsuccessful.
There are still zero ordinary failures
and zero errors.
A dashboard that adds only those two
fields would miss the problem.
The framework is signaling that a
maintained expectation is stale. The
test no longer behaves as the marker
says.
Investigate whether the underlying issue
was fixed or whether the test stopped
checking it.
Remove or change the marker only after
understanding that change.
A passing body is useful evidence, but
reporting it under an outdated exception
is not a clean result.
Read unexpected successes explicitly
instead of burying them in a green
summary.
Compare two one method cases. The first
makes a false equality assertion and
records one failure.
The second raises value error and
records one error.
Both overall results are unsuccessful,
but their diagnostic meaning differs.
The first says a checked expectation did
not match. The second says execution
encountered an exception outside the
expected assertion handling.
Do not rename every red result of failed
comparison.
Also, avoid assuming that every
exception is an error in every context.
An assertion that correctly expects an
exception can pass. We will test that
boundary later.
Start with the exact case, its exception
type, and the result field that changed.
Classification helps locate the problem,
while the traceback and test intent
explain what repair is appropriate.
Our test method loops through one, two,
and three.
Each row has a sub test and checks
whether the number is even. Rows one and
three fail, while row two passes.
Without fail fast, all three rows are
attempted.
The result reports tests run equal to
one because it ran one test method, but
records two failure entries for the
failing sub tests.
Therefore, dividing failures by tests
run can produce a misleading picture.
A method count and a sub test problem
count are not the same unit.
Sub tests help preserve row context and
continue independent checks in this
example. They do not automatically make
every row a separate collected test
case.
State whether your report counts
methods, parameter rows, or assertion
events before comparing totals.
Run the same sub test method with fail
fast enabled. The first row fails, the
stop flag becomes true, and our event
list contains only one.
Rows two and three were not attempted.
The method counter is still one, and the
failure count is now one.
It would be wrong to describe this as
fewer bugs simply because the report
contains fewer failures. We changed the
execution policy so there was less
opportunity to observe them.
Fail fast can shorten a feedback loop,
but it trades a fuller diagnostic pass
for an earlier stop.
When comparing two reports, keep runner
settings alongside the counts. A change
in configuration can explain a smaller
report without any change to the
behavior under test.
Our setup records an event, registers
two cleanup functions, then raises
runtime error.
The test body never runs and teardown is
not called because setup did not
succeed.
Yet tests run is one and the result has
one error.
Again, the counter does not certify body
execution.
This case matters when a database
connection, temporary resource, or
fixture construction fails before the
assertion you expected to see.
Do not chase a missing assertion failure
until you check whether the test reached
that assertion at all.
The output and our event log make the
path explicit.
We use only local synthetic events here,
so there are no external resources to
leak.
The same lifecycle distinction is worth
understanding before adding real
resources.
After that setup error, the registered
cleanup functions still run.
Our event list is setup, cleanup second,
cleanup first.
Registration order and execution order
are reversed, last in, first out.
This is the behavior we verified, not a
guess based on the word cleanup.
Register a cleanup when the
corresponding resource has been acquired
successfully, so a later setup failure
does not strand it.
A cleanup registered after the failing
statement would never have been
registered.
Also, calling a cleanup function is not
itself proof that a remote deletion or
close operation succeeded.
Our example appends to a list and the
harness checks the exact list.
For real resources, observe the cleanup
result at the appropriate boundary
rather than extending this local
guarantee.
Now setup succeeds. The body records its
event and fails an equality assertion.
Teardown then runs and raises runtime
error while the registered cleanup still
records its event afterward.
The result has one test run, one
failure, and one error.
Adding failures and errors gives two
problems not two executed test methods.
This is another reason a dashboard
cannot assume every result entry belongs
to a different test.
The body problem and the fixture problem
both deserve attention.
Fixing the assertion alone would leave
teardown broken. Fixing teardown alone
would leave the false assertion.
Preserve both diagnostics and the
lifecycle sequence instead of collapsing
them into whichever red message you
happen to notice first.
Our harness checks the exact order and
both result categories.
Put the expected failure decorator on
the test method but let setup raise
before the method starts.
Our result records an error, not an
expected failure, and overall success is
false.
The method marker does not turn every
possible fixture problem into an
accepted failure.
That scope is important when a known
application bug coexists with a broken
environment or fixture.
Calling all of it expected would hide a
different problem.
In our example, the method body would
deliberately fail too but it never gets
the chance.
Read where the exception occurred, not
only which decorator appears above the
method.
A maintained exception should cover the
intended known behavior while
independent setup and cleanup failures
remain visible for diagnosis.
Our class defines test underscore one,
test two, and check underscore three.
The default loader collects the first
two because their names start with test
and underscore is a convention, not the
default requirement.
The helper beginning with check is
excluded.
This is a collection observation before
running the suite.
Count test cases answers how many cases
the suite contains at that point, not
how many bodies later complete.
Do not equate a list of collected names
with a finished execution report.
Check the selected class and names when
a test disappears, but remember that the
loader itself is configurable.
We will deliberately change the prefix
next, so the same class leads to a
different selected set without editing
its method bodies.
Create a fresh test loader and set its
test method prefix to check.
Loading the same class now selects only
check underscore three.
Our harness verifies the selected name
and the count of one.
The methods did not change, the policy
did.
This is why universal claims such as
unit test only runs names starting with
test need their default loader
qualification.
It is also why a test count comparison
across configurations needs care.
A smaller selected suite may be
deliberate or it may be the mistake you
need to catch.
Keep a record of the command, selector,
and loader settings that produced the
report.
Naming conventions are useful
agreements, but they are not immutable
rules of every custom test runner or
suite.
Our method uses assert raises with value
error, raises that exact exception, then
checks its message.
The result succeeds with no recorded
error.
The exception happened, but the test
explicitly expected and handled it
through an assertion.
This is different from letting value
error escape the method unexpectedly.
Keep the asserted block as narrow as the
behavior you mean.
If a large setup block can raise the
same exception type for an unrelated
reason, a broad exception assertion may
pass without reaching the intended
operation.
Our small fixture avoids that ambiguity
and also checks the message.
A message check has its own maintenance
cost, so use it when the exact
diagnostic is part of the contract
rather than copying it mechanically into
every test.
Use the same assertion, but let its
block do nothing.
No value error occurs, so the assertion
fails. One failure, zero errors.
Now let type error escape inside the
value error assertion.
wrong exception is not accepted, and our
result records one error instead.
These two red outcomes point to
different mismatches.
One says the promised exception never
happened. The other says a different
exception happened.
Neither should be repaired by catching
every exception until the report turns
green.
Decide which error type the behavior is
meant to expose and keep the fixture
narrow enough to demonstrate that
contract.
Our harness checks both classifications
separately, so a change that
accidentally broadens the exception
handling would be visible in the
teaching lab.
For this lab, we define a deliberately
strict teaching gate. At least one test,
overall successful, zero skipped, and
zero expected failures.
It rejects the empty, all skipped, and
expected failure examples, accepts our
shown passing case, and rejects the
unexpected success through the success
field.
This is our policy, not a built-in
definition of good testing.
A project may legitimately allow
documented skips or known failures under
its own rules.
More importantly, even our stricter gate
can accept a useless test with no
meaningful assertion. It does not
measure coverage, prove the selected
suite is correct, or certify an
integration.
Use a gate to enforce explicit minimum
conditions, then keep test quality and
coverage questions separate.
Finish by naming the selected suite, the
runner settings, and the claim you want
the result to support.
Was work merely collected, counted,
skipped, or actually executed?
Our failures, errors, expected failures,
and unexpected successes all visible.
Did subtests or fixture errors create
more result entries than method
executions?
Did fail fast stop later work?
Were cleanups registered before setup
could fail?
Our 60 harness checks verify these exact
Python 3.10 local fixtures, including
intentionally unsuccessful inner runs.
They do not certify your application or
every Python version.
Read the official documentation beside
the runnable example and rerun it in the
environment you use.
A useful report preserves missing work
and known exceptions instead of
polishing them away.
Green is a result to interpret, not a
reason to stop thinking.
